title: Marguerite and the House
premise: Mirabel Montrose, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise the derelict Aldous House and discovers it responds to measurement — rooms shift, dimensions lie, and her own sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud. The voice belongs to Marguerite, a woman taken by the house in 1974, whose name Mirabel has been unknowingly carrying in her family's silence for fifty years. As the harvest moon approaches, Mirabel learns the house feeds on belonging: it keeps what loves it, and it has decided to keep her. To survive, she must return what was stolen in 1974 — Marguerite's recorded confession of the house's true nature, hidden inside a wall — and speak her family's complicity aloud, trading her claim on the house for Marguerite's release. In the end, Mirabel walks out with an appraisal that reads simply: not for sale, never was.
about_author: E. M. Nystrom is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing structural anomalies in rural properties before turning to fiction. They write horror about houses that remember, drawing on archival research and a lifelong unease with basements.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Mirabel accepts an appraisal job on Aldous House from a law firm that won't say who the client is. POV: Mirabel. The beat is professional detachment masking a hunger to belong somewhere after years of transient work; she photographs every room like a promise she intends to keep.

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: First survey day: the exterior measurements refuse to reconcile, off by eleven feet no matter how many times she recalculates. POV: Mirabel. The emotional beat is the first crack in her rationalism — irritation curdling into fascination as the house seems to be measuring her back.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Room
chapters.summary: Mirabel finds a bedroom sealed with fresh paint over old wallpaper, monogrammed 'M.A.' Local records list a Marguerite Aldous, missing since 1974. POV: Mirabel. The beat is reluctant tenderness; she begins speaking to the empty room out of habit, then out of something warmer.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Mirabel sets up audio recorders to log settling sounds overnight, framing it as thoroughness. She narrates her findings aloud to the recorder like a litany. POV: Mirabel. The beat is ritual comfort — her logs are how she makes an indifferent world hold still.

chapters.title: Playback
chapters.summary: Reviewing the night recording, Mirabel hears a second voice — low, patient, female — answering questions from her own half-asleep murmuring. It knows things about her childhood. POV: Mirabel. The beat is vertigo; her system of documentation has become a channel she cannot close.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Night three: the voice introduces itself as Marguerite and asks Mirabel to bring 'the tape' back to the house. Mirabel, terrified, plays along and asks what tape. POV: alternating Mirabel and transcribed recordings. The beat is dread braided with longing — the voice is kind, and that is worse.

chapters.title: What the County Clerk Kept
chapters.summary: Mirabel digs through 1974 archives: Marguerite Aldous, twenty-six, vanished during a house survey conducted by — Mirabel's grandfather. POV: Mirabel. The beat is betrayal; her inheritance isn't just a surname but complicity, and the house has been waiting for the family to return.

chapters.title: Rooms That Rearrange
chapters.summary: Mirabel returns to find hallways lengthened and the sealed bedroom now directly across from where she sleeps. Her tools read impossible values; her camera shows figures in doorways. POV: Mirabel. The beat is claustrophobic escalation — the house is rearranging itself around her like a hand closing.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Calendar
chapters.summary: Marguerite's voice explains the house harvests on the full moon nearest the equinox — six days away — and that it keeps whoever it has grown to love. Mirabel realizes she's been courted. POV: Mirabel. The beat is horrified clarity: every kindness the house showed her was appetite.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Ledger
chapters.summary: In her late grandfather's effects, Mirabel finds his 1974 field ledger: the final entry describes removing a reel-to-reel tape from behind Marguerite's wallpaper and 'securing it for the firm.' POV: Mirabel. The beat is grief and fury — her family didn't just witness the taking; they armed it.

chapters.title: The Firm
chapters.summary: Mirabel confronts the law firm; a dying senior partner admits the 'client' is a trust that has kept Aldous House fed with appraisers for fifty years. He begs her to walk away. POV: Mirabel. The beat is moral crisis — walking away means leaving Marguerite, and the next surveyor, to the house.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: Mirabel tries to quit; the house retaliates by making her apartment feel wrong, thin, unlived-in, while Aldous House appears warm in her dreams. POV: Mirabel. The beat is seduction — belonging, she understands now, is exactly the hook the house uses, and it fits her perfectly.

chapters.title: Questions at Night
chapters.summary: Mirabel interrogates the recordings systematically, learning the house answers any question asked aloud within its walls — including questions about her. It has been studying her since childhood visits to her grandfather. POV: Mirabel and transcripts. The beat is violation; her identity itself feels surveyed.

chapters.title: Marguerite Speaks Plainly
chapters.summary: In a long nocturnal conversation, Marguerite recounts 1974: she documented the house too, hid her tape in the wall, and was taken mid-sentence. She asks Mirabel to finish her sentence. POV: Marguerite via recording, framed by Mirabel. The beat is intimacy across death — two documenters, one unfinished record.

chapters.title: The Tape
chapters.summary: Mirabel traces the reel to a bank deposit box held by the trust, and steals it during a storm, triggering alarms and the partner's warning call. POV: Mirabel. The beat is decisive transgression — loyalty shifts from institutions to the dead woman who deserves the truth spoken.

chapters.title: Two Nights Before
chapters.summary: Mirabel listens to Marguerite's 1974 tape: a calm, complete account of the house's nature, cut off by a sound like a door opening inward. The house, listening through her recorder, goes silent for the first time. POV: Mirabel. The beat is terrible stillness — the predator knows its prey has found the recipe.

chapters.title: The House Argues
chapters.summary: The house stops pretending: doors seal, walls breathe, and it offers Mirabel everything she's ever wanted — permanence, purpose, a room of her own — if she stays willingly. POV: Mirabel. The beat is temptation at full strength; she must name what belonging really costs.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Mirabel enters with the tape, a hammer, and her grandfather's ledger, and opens the wall behind Marguerite's wallpaper as the house screams through every pipe. POV: Mirabel. The beat is grim resolve — she returns the truth to the place it was buried, reading Marguerite's words aloud into the dark.

chapters.title: The Taking, Reversed
chapters.summary: Under the rising harvest moon, the house tries to take Mirabel instead; Marguerite's released voice turns the house's own hunger against it, naming it as the thing that doesn't belong. POV: Mirabel, fragmenting. The beat is climax — truth as exorcism, spoken in two voices until the walls stop answering.

chapters.title: Dawn Appraisal
chapters.summary: Mirabel wakes on the lawn at sunrise; the house stands ordinary, small, finally just a house. Her final survey measures true for the first time. POV: Mirabel. The beat is exhausted peace — the numbers reconcile because nothing inside is lying anymore.

chapters.title: Not For Sale
chapters.summary: Mirabel files her report recommending demolition and donates the land to the county as a memorial to Marguerite Aldous, whose disappearance is reopened as a homicide. POV: Mirabel. The beat is restitution — she can't undo 1974, but she can make the record honest.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: Weeks later, playing her old tapes one final time before archiving them, Mirabel hears Marguerite's voice add one new line: thank you, and a question — will you remember me? Mirabel answers aloud, alone, and files the tape under her own name beside Marguerite's. POV: Mirabel. The beat is bittersweet closure — belonging, chosen freely, given to the dead.
